Abraham Maslow expose sa hiérarchie des: Abraham Maslow set out his hierarchy of needs in 1943 in Psychological Review. He never drew a pyramid: it is due to consultant Charles McDermid, in the journal Business Horizons.
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi part de l'observ: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi started from watching painters, so absorbed they forgot hunger and fatigue. He described flow in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975), then in a popular book in 1990.
Edwin Locke lance la théorie de la fixat: Edwin Locke launched goal-setting theory in 1968. With Gary Latham, he summarised it in 1990 and again in 2002, from about 400 studies.
La première expérience a lieu en 1970 à: The first experiment took place in 1970 at Stanford's Bing Nursery School. A 1990 follow-up linked waiting to better SAT scores, but a 2018 replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found much smaller effects.
Le mot vient du latin procrastinare, de: The word comes from the Latin procrastinare, from cras, "tomorrow". Psychologist Piers Steel defined it in 2007 as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action despite expecting to be worse off.
Bluma Zeigarnik publie en 1927 dans Psyc: Bluma Zeigarnik published in 1927 in Psychologische Forschung, after Kurt Lewin noticed that a waiter remembered orders only until they were paid. A 2025 meta-analysis found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks.
L'idée vient des recherches de Carol Dwe: The idea comes from Carol Dweck's research at Stanford. Large classroom trials have been disappointing: the Education Endowment Foundation's in 2019, then a 2024 study, found no gain.
En 2009, Phillippa Lally suit des volont: In 2009, Phillippa Lally followed volunteers: on average it took them 66 days for an action to become automatic, from 18 to 254 depending on the case. William James already said we are "bundles of habits".
Solomon Asch mène ses expériences en 195: Solomon Asch ran his experiments in 1951 at Swarthmore College. 74% of participants went along with the group's wrong answer at least once; with a single ally in the room, they gave in only 5% of the time.
Stanley Milgram commence en août 1961, t: Stanley Milgram began in August 1961, three months after the trial of Adolf Eichmann opened in Jerusalem: he wanted to understand how ordinary people obey atrocious orders. He published in 1963.
Dans la version de base, 65 % des partic: In the baseline version, 65% of participants went up to 450 volts. Jerry Burger in 2009 found similar rates, halting after the 150-volt switch; Gina Perry, in 2012, reported a troubling mismatch between the published descriptions and what actually happened.
L'idée naît du meurtre de Kitty Genovese: The idea was born from the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York on 13 March 1964, whose story of neighbours who stayed passive was exaggerated: The New York Times itself acknowledged it in 2016. In 2019, Richard Philpot showed from street videos that someone intervened in over 90% of conflicts.
Edward Thorndike nomme l'effet en 1920 :: Edward Thorndike named the effect in 1920: officers rated their soldiers good or bad at everything at once. In 1972, Karen Dion and colleagues showed that people credit attractive faces with more qualities.
Leon Festinger publie sa théorie en 1957: Leon Festinger published his theory in 1957. With James Carlsmith, he showed that students paid $1 to praise a boring task ended up finding it more enjoyable than those paid $20.
En 1966, Jonathan Freedman et Scott Fras: In 1966, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser asked residents to accept a large sign in their yard: 76% said yes after a small prior request, against 17% without.
En 1971, Dennis Regan montre que des par: In 1971, Dennis Regan showed that participants given a soft drink later bought more raffle tickets. Sociologist Phillip Kunz sent greeting cards to strangers: many sent one back.
En 1975, Stephen Worchel et ses collègue: In 1975, Stephen Worchel and colleagues offered cookies from a jar: those from a jar holding only 2 were rated better than those from a jar holding 10.
Tout part du mémoire de master de James: It all started with James Stoner's master's thesis at MIT in 1961, on the "risky shift" of groups. Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni generalised the effect in 1969: the group pushes in the direction it already leaned.
William Whyte forge le mot groupthink en: William Whyte coined the word groupthink in 1952 in Fortune magazine. Irving Janis studied it through fiascos such as the Bay of Pigs invasion; the decision to launch the Challenger shuttle is another example often cited.
En août 1971, 24 étudiants jouent gardie: In August 1971, 24 students played guards and prisoners; the experiment, planned for two weeks, was stopped on day 6 after Christina Maslach intervened. In 2018, Thibault Le Texier argued in Histoire d'un mensonge that the guards' behaviour was caused by Zimbardo's instructions.
Le chiffre de 86 milliards vient de Suza: The figure of 86 billion comes from Suzana Herculano-Houzel: in 2005 she developed a method that dissolves the brain into a "soup" of cell nuclei that can be counted.
Le mythe se répand en 1936, dans la préf: The myth spread in 1936, in Lowell Thomas's foreword to Dale Carnegie's book, which attributed the figure to William James. It is wrongly attributed to Einstein. Brain imaging shows that every region is active.
Le 13 septembre 1848, à Cavendish (Vermo: On 13 September 1848, in Cavendish, Vermont, an iron bar 1.1 m long and weighing 6 kg went through the skull of this railroad foreman. According to his doctor John Harlow, he was "no longer Gage". Yet he ended up a stagecoach driver in Chile and died on 21 May 1860.
Paul Broca examine en 1861 le cerveau de: In 1861, Paul Broca examined the brain of Louis Victor Leborgne, nicknamed "Tan", the only word he could say: a lesion of the left frontal lobe. Physician Marc Dax had made a similar observation a generation earlier.
Santiago Ramón y Cajal colore les neuron: Santiago Ramón y Cajal stained neurons with Camillo Golgi's method, though Golgi believed in a continuous network. They shared the Nobel Prize in 1906, and Cajal's drawings are still used in textbooks.
Le mythe vient d'une lecture abusive des: The myth comes from an overstretched reading of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga's 1960s studies of split-brain patients. In 2013, a University of Utah study found no "dominant side" in individuals.
William James parle de plasticité dès 18: William James spoke of plasticity as early as 1890, and Pole Jerzy Konorski was the first to write "neural plasticity". Paul Bach-y-Rita showed that people can learn to "see" through touch.
Eleanor Maguire a observé chez les chauf: Eleanor Maguire observed changes in the hippocampus of London taxi drivers, the region for memory of places.
Seiji Ogawa découvre le signal BOLD en 1: Seiji Ogawa discovered the BOLD signal in 1990 at Bell Labs. The idea is old: Angelo Mosso already weighed blood flow to the brain, and Charles Roy and Charles Sherrington linked activity and blood flow in 1890. In 2009, a dead salmon "responded" in a badly analysed scan.
Le neurochirurgien Wilder Penfield opère: Neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield operated on awake patients under local anaesthesia, a technique learned in Germany in 1928. By stimulating their cortex, he mapped the body's "little man", the homunculus. He founded the Montreal Neurological Institute in 1934.
Cervelet veut dire « petit cerveau ». Ga: Cerebellum means "little brain". Galen already described it; Luigi Rolando in 1809, then Pierre Flourens showed its role in movement. It holds more neurons than all the rest of the brain.
Chez Binet, à Paris, Jean Piaget corrige: At Binet's in Paris, Jean Piaget marked intelligence tests and became interested in children's mistakes. He then closely observed his own three children, and founded the International Centre for Genetic Epistemology in Geneva in 1955.
Jean Piaget tire ses quatre stades en bo: Jean Piaget drew his four stages largely from observing his own three children.
Piaget décrit « l'erreur A-non-B » : le: Piaget described the "A-not-B error": the baby looks for the toy where it found it before, not where it saw it hidden. In 1991, Renée Baillargeon and Julie DeVos showed that a baby of three and a half months is already surprised when a hidden object vanishes.
En 1985, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie: In 1985, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie and Uta Frith ran the test: 85% of non-autistic children passed (23 of 27), against 20% of autistic children (4 of 20).
Lev Vygotski introduit cette notion dans: Lev Vygotsky introduced this idea in the last three years of his life, before his death in 1934. The word "scaffolding", often linked to it, came later from Jerome Bruner, David Wood and Gail Ross.
Harry Harlow présente ses résultats en 1: Harry Harlow presented his results in 1958 in "The Nature of Love": baby monkeys preferred the cloth mother to the wire mother that gave milk. These experiments are now considered unethical.
Le psychiatre John Bowlby pose la théori: Psychiatrist John Bowlby set out the theory, and Mary Ainsworth devised the "Strange Situation" in the 1970s, observing a baby's reaction when its mother leaves and comes back.
Selon Piaget, la conservation s'acquiert: According to Piaget, conservation is acquired around age 7. But when a "naughty teddy" messes up the row, in James McGarrigle and Margaret Donaldson's experiment, younger children succeed far more often.
Janet Werker et Richard Tees le montrent: Janet Werker and Richard Tees showed it: at 6-8 months, babies tell apart the sounds of a foreign language better than at 8-10 months, when their ear has already tuned to the language they hear.
En 1993, Frances Rauscher fait écouter M: In 1993, Frances Rauscher played Mozart to 36 students (not babies): a slight gain on a spatial task, lasting about fifteen minutes. Georgia governor Zell Miller nonetheless proposed in 1998 to give every newborn a classical music CD. Meta-analyses by Chabris (1999) and Pietschnig (2010) found no notable effect.
Eleanor Gibson et Richard Walk testent 3: Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk tested 36 babies aged 6 to 14 months; 27 of them crawled to their mother on the shallow side. More recent work indicates that this caution is not innate: it comes with experience.
Francis Galton propose dès 1884 de cherc: Francis Galton proposed as early as 1884 looking for traits in the words of the language. In 1936, Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert listed 4,504 adjectives. Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal found five factors in 1961, and Lewis Goldberg named them the "Big Five" in 1981.
Katharine Briggs et sa fille Isabel Myer: Katharine Briggs and her daughter Isabel Myers, with no training in psychology, drew on Jung (1921) and began during the Second World War; the manual came out in 1962. Between 39 and 76% of people get a different type when retaking it five weeks later.
Le névrosisme fait partie des cinq facte: Neuroticism is one of the five factors found by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal in 1961, which Lewis Goldberg named the "Big Five" in 1981.
Pour Hans Eysenck, l'introverti a un cer: For Hans Eysenck, the introvert has an already highly aroused brain and seeks less stimulation. In 2012, Susan Cain's book Quiet popularised the defence of introverts.
Carl Jung les introduit dans Psychologis: Carl Jung introduced them in Psychologische Typen in 1921, translated into English in 1923.
Delroy Paulhus et Kevin Williams nomment: Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams named the dark triad in 2002. Machiavellianism was already measured with Richard Christie and Florence Geis's MACH-IV scale (1970). Sadism is sometimes added: the "dark tetrad".
La théorie des quatre humeurs vient d'Hi: The theory of the four humours comes from Hippocrates; Galen drew from it the four temperaments: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic. Kant still used them in 1798.
Franz Joseph Gall lance sa « cranioscopi: Franz Joseph Gall launched his "cranioscopy" around 1796; his collaborator Johann Spurzheim popularised the word "phrenology". Pierre Flourens's experiments helped discredit it by the 1840s.
À partir de 1979, Thomas Bouchard étudie: From 1979, Thomas Bouchard studied identical twins raised apart in Minneapolis: they are about 50% alike in personality.
Lee Ross nomme cette erreur en 1977, d'a: Lee Ross named this error in 1977, based on Edward Jones and Victor Harris's experiment (1967): even knowing a writer had been assigned to argue for Fidel Castro, readers credited the writer with that opinion.
Le modèle des Big Five vient de Tupes et: The Big Five model comes from Tupes and Christal (1961) and Goldberg (1981); of the five traits, conscientiousness best predicts exam success.
En 1936, Hans Selye publie « A Syndrome: In 1936, Hans Selye published "A Syndrome Produced by Diverse Nocuous Agents": he observed that rats exposed to cold, drugs or injury all reacted the same way, in three phases. He later distinguished good stress (eustress) from bad (distress).
Robert Yerkes et John Dodson publient en: Robert Yerkes and John Dodson published in 1908 in the Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, from experiments on dancing mice. The paper was cited only ten times in fifty years before becoming famous.
L'étude commence en 1938 à la faculté de: The study began in 1938 at Harvard Medical School, funded by William Thomas Grant, with 268 students. George Vaillant directed it for more than thirty years; Robert Waldinger took over. One of its conclusions: success depends on warmth of relationships, not on intelligence.
Philip Brickman et Donald Campbell parle: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell spoke of the "hedonic treadmill" in 1971. In 1978, Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman compared 22 lottery winners and 29 paraplegics: the winners were no happier than before, and the paraplegics expected to get back to their level within a couple of years.
Martin Seligman en fait le thème de sa p: Martin Seligman made it the theme of his term as president of the American Psychological Association in 1998, feeling the field focused too much on illness. The phrase dates back at least to 1954, the title of a chapter by Maslow.
En 1967, à l'université de Pennsylvanie,: In 1967, at the University of Pennsylvania, dogs that had no way to stop shocks later lay down in a box they could have escaped with one jump. In 2016, Steven Maier and Seligman turned the theory around: by default the brain assumes it has no control, and it is control that is learned.
Le record est détenu par Randy Gardner,: The record belongs to Randy Gardner, who stayed awake 264 hours, 11 days, without stimulants. The US National Sleep Foundation recommends that adults aim for 7 hours a night.
Jon Kabat-Zinn crée son programme de réd: Jon Kabat-Zinn created his stress reduction programme in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. It lasts eight weeks; its roots are in Zen Buddhism, but the programme is secular.
Le psychologue Herbert Freudenberger s'o: Psychologist Herbert Freudenberger observed himself and his fellow volunteers at a free clinic for drug addicts, in "Staff Burn-Out" in 1974. Christina Maslach published her inventory in 1981, and the WHO recognised it in 2019 as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition.
En 1986, James Pennebaker et Sandra Beal: In 1986, James Pennebaker and Sandra Beall had students write 15 minutes a day, 4 days in a row, about their deepest thoughts on a trauma. Over the following months, they visited the doctor significantly less than those who wrote about neutral topics.
